source: queens-gambit.json :: Chapter 5: The Queen's Gambit Accepted (promoted to its own opening)
intro: WELCOME. This is a realistic-opponent repertoire for the Queen's Gambit complex (1.d4 d5 2.c4), built the same way as the companion Sicilian Defense Encyclopedia: for every position, the main theoretical moves, common tries you'll actually meet, sharp/gambit lines, quiet positional systems, traps, and typical mistakes. PLANNED TABLE OF CONTENTS — Chapter 1: Understanding the Queen's Gambit (foundations — structures, breaks, plans). Chapter 2: The Queen's Gambit Declined, Main Lines (Orthodox). Chapter 3: The Exchange Variation and the Minority Attack. Chapter 4: The Tartakower, Lasker, and Cambridge Springs Defenses. Chapter 5: The Queen's Gambit Accepted. Chapter 6: The Slav Defense. Chapter 7: The Semi-Slav (Meran, Botvinnik, Moscow). Chapter 8: The Catalan. Chapter 9: The Chigorin, Albin Countergambit, and Other Rare Black Tries. Chapter 10: Traps and Tactics Compendium. Chapters will be built and appended one at a time, exactly as with the Sicilian book, with every line verified move-by-move for legality and spot-checked against current theory before being added.

THE FURMAN VARIATION — an important alternative to 6.O-O, with a specific idea: rather than allowing Black to trade queens after a later ...cxd4/...Qxd4-type exchange, White keeps the queens on and aims for a symmetrical-looking structure with real attacking chances via a later e4-e5 push.
the point — resolving the center immediately while the queen is well-placed on e2 to support the coming central expansion.
striking in the center with real force now that development is complete.
A very precise, well-known equalizing resource — offering a trade of knights to defuse White's central ambitions before they can fully materialize.

and Black has successfully held back White's e4-e5 ambitions while completing development with fully equal chances — this exact sequence was demonstrated in a famous Radjabov-Kasparov game and remains the main practical answer to White's sharpest try in this whole variation.

and White has regained the gambit pawn AND won the exchange, all because Black tried to hold onto material without adequate preparation — this exact "grab and hold without central support" mistake is one of the most common ways club and online players misplay the Queen's Gambit Accepted.
